name: Mehndi bridal ceremony

lead: Mehndi is the South Asian name for henna body art, and the bridal mehndi ceremony is a pre-wedding celebration in which the bride, and sometimes her guests, receive elaborate designs on the hands and feet. The paste, made from powdered leaves of Lawsonia inermis, leaves a temporary reddish-brown stain.

The visual payoff is ornamented hands and feet for the wedding and its photographs. Henna practices of this kind are documented from the Mediterranean and Middle East to South Asia, and UNESCO inscribed henna rituals and aesthetic practices on its Intangible Cultural Heritage list in December 2024.

paras: Dried henna leaves are milled, mixed with a liquid such as water, lemon juice or tea, and left to rest to release the dye. Artists pipe the paste through a cone in floral or geometric patterns, and it is left on for several hours, often overnight, then removed dry. The stain starts orange and darkens over about three days, then fades within one to three weeks; palms and soles stain darkest.

Pure henna has few reported side effects, but products sold as black henna often contain para-phenylenediamine (PPD), which has caused blistering, scarring and lasting sensitisation, with reactions appearing days after application. The FDA has not approved henna for direct skin application, and henna is hazardous for people with G6PD deficiency.

angle.text: The ceremony gives the bride temporary patterned skin art that deepens over days. Designs run from simple dots to dense arabesques, and the stain lasts one to three weeks.

lead: Mehndi is the Hindi and Urdu word for henna, the reddish dye from the leaves of Lawsonia inermis, and the mehndi ceremony or henna night is the pre-wedding event at which a bride's hands and feet are decorated with temporary designs. [1][2]

The look it creates is detailed floral and geometric ornament in warm brown-red, applied before the wedding so the stain has time to deepen. Traditions describe darker stains as an omen of a happy marriage. [1] The custom exists in many regions: Pakistan's Rasm-e-Heena, Tunisian celebrations beginning eight days before the wedding, Moroccan festivals of up to five days, and Ottoman henna nights (kina gecesi). [1][2]
Research on the practice is mostly dermatological: reviews of its globalisation and case reports of reactions to adulterated 'black henna'. [3][4][5]

paras: The paste is made from dried, powdered henna leaves mixed with liquids such as water, lemon juice or tea and rested from one to 48 hours to release lawsone. Sugar or molasses helps it adhere, and some essential oils improve staining. [2][1]

It is usually left on at least four to six hours, often overnight, and removed dry rather than with water. The stain begins orange, darkens to reddish brown over about three days and fades in one to three weeks, darkest on the thick skin of palms and soles. [2]

Henna was used in ancient Egypt on hair, skin and nails, and wall paintings at Akrotiri show markings consistent with henna on women's hands and feet. Wikipedia reports that henna has adorned brides and grooms since the late Bronze Age in the eastern Mediterranean, with the Ugaritic legend of Baal and Anath the earliest text linking henna to marriage. [2]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, traces mehndi's Sanskrit root mendhika and describes elaboration of South Asian designs under the Mughal Empire in the 16th century. [1] Henna is also used at Eid, Diwali, Purim and Passover, and on December 3, 2024 UNESCO inscribed 'Henna, rituals, aesthetic and social practices'. [2]

In Hindu traditions the ceremony is said to bring prosperity, fertility and marital bliss, and a darker stain is read as a sign of a happy marriage; among Muslim and Jewish communities henna marks joy and protection at weddings and festivals. [1]

'Black henna' usually contains no henna and may carry PPD, a hair-dye chemical, in concentrations reported from 10% to 80%; hair dyes are limited to under 6%. Reactions typically appear 3 to 12 days after application and can cause blistering, scarring and lifelong sensitisation. [2] A 2020 case report described a mixed bullous-eczematous dermatitis from a black henna tattoo, and a 2017 report described acute forearm compartment syndrome after artificial mehndi dermatitis. [4][5]

The US FDA has not approved henna for direct skin application, and henna is hazardous in G6PD deficiency, particularly for infants and children. [2] A 2023 letter also reported a reflex epilepsy triggered by the smell of mehndi. [6]

No trials of the ceremony as an appearance treatment have been published. Related literature includes a 2020 dermatology review of globalised cultural practices such as mehndi and bindi, a 2003 mouse study of henna leaf extract on enzyme systems and chemically induced skin tumours, and the case reports above. [3][7][4][5]
